# Open Payments

## What is Open Payments?

Open Payments is an open API standard that can be implemented by account servicing entities (e.g. banks, digital wallet providers, and mobile money providers) to facilitate interoperability in the setup and completion of payments for different use cases including:

- [Web Monetization](https://webmonetization.org)
- Tipping/Donations (low value/low friction)
- eCommerce checkout
- P2P transfers
- Subscriptions
- Invoice Payments

The Open Payments APIs are a collection of three sub-systems:

- A **wallet address server** which exposes public information about Open Payments-enabled accounts called "wallet addresses"
- A **resource server** which exposes APIs for performing functions against the underlying accounts
- A **authorisation server** which exposes APIs compliant with the [GNAP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-gnap-core-protocol) standard for getting grants to access the resource server APIs

This repository contains contains a [NodeJS Open Payments SDK](https://github.com/interledger/open-payments-node/tree/main/packages/open-payments) to make requests via the Open Payments API, as well as TypeScript types for the API.

It also contains two additional libraries:

- [`@interledger/http-signature-utils`](https://github.com/interledger/open-payments/tree/main/packages/http-signature-utils) provides tools for working with [HTTP Message Signatures](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-message-signatures).
- [`@interledger/openapi`](https://github.com/interledger/open-payments/tree/main/packages/openapi) exposes functionality to validate requests and responses according to a given OpenAPI 3.1 schema.

### New to Interledger?

Never heard of Interledger before? Or would you like to learn more? Here are some excellent places to start:

- [Interledger Website](https://interledger.org/)
- [Interledger Specification](https://interledger.org/developers/rfcs/interledger-protocol/)
- [Interledger Explainer Video](https://twitter.com/Interledger/status/1567916000074678272)
- [Open Payments](https://openpayments.dev/)
- [Web monetization](https://webmonetization.org/)

## Contributing

Please read the [contribution guidelines](.github/contributing.md) before submitting contributions. All contributions must adhere to our [code of conduct](.github/code_of_conduct.md).

## Open Payments Community Call

Our Community Calls are open to everyone in our community. We have them every other Thursday at 13:00 GMT, via Google Meet.

Video call link: https://meet.google.com/fcb-xamx-csr

[Add to Google Calendar](https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MG1tYzlwOHVtMmg5dnQxOXNodWc4czdxdG5fMjAyNjA1MDdUMTIwMDAwWiBiaWJpYW5hQGludGVybGVkZ2VyLm9yZw&tmsrc=bibiana%40interledger.org&scp=ALL)

## Local Development Environment

This repository contains a Git submodule, which contains the Open Payments OpenAPI specifications.
After cloning, make sure to initialize and update it:

```bash
git submodule update --init
```

Alternatively, clone the repository with submodules in one step:

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:interledger/open-payments-node.git
```

### Prerequisites

- [NVM](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm)

### Environment Setup

```sh
# install node from `./.nvmrc`
nvm install

# install pnpm
corepack enable

# if moving from yarn run
pnpm clean

# install dependencies
pnpm i
```

### Useful commands

```sh
# format and lint code:
pnpm format

# check lint and formatting
pnpm checks

# verify code formatting:
pnpm check:prettier

# verify lint
pnpm check:lint

# build all the packages in the repo:
pnpm -r build

# run individual tests (e.g. open-payments)
pnpm --filter open-payments test

# run all tests
pnpm -r --workspace-concurrency=1 test
```

4. **AI disclosure (required):**
   - An `AI_USAGE.md` file in the repo root listing the tools you used, what for, and in which files. It should also name the files written with little or no AI, such as the Open Payments service.
   - A `/prompts/` folder with the **actual prompt text** you sent. Since I'm one of those tools, the prompts you send me count too.

Optional extras: architecture diagrams, mockups, technical docs.

## Judging
- **Criteria:** problem definition, Open Payments usage (a working payment flow), user experience, technical quality, presentation, inclusion, innovation, impact. Each is scored 0–5.
- **Round 1 at 12:00:** a 5-minute pitch plus demo in front of at least 2 judges.
- **Round 2:** the top 12 teams pitch again, also 5 minutes.
- **Prizes** (about USD 5k each, paid in COP, max one prize per team):
  - Impact (RutaN)
  - Inclusion (Puntored)
  - Innovation (FIND EAFIT)
  - Community (This Week in Fintech, voted by participants)
- **Disqualification:** not using the Open Payments API, or using code written before the event.

## Technology
- **Stack:** you can use any language. The official SDK is `@interledger/open-payments`, currently v7.4.0, for Node/TypeScript. There's also a PHP SDK.
- **Test wallet:** sign up at [wallet.interledger-test.dev](https://wallet.interledger-test.dev). Create wallet addresses, then generate a developer key pair there to get a key ID and private key.
- **The standard flow:**
  1. Resolve the wallet addresses.
  2. Get an incoming-payment grant, then create the incoming payment on the receiver.
  3. Get a quote grant, then create the quote on the sender.
  4. Get an **interactive** outgoing-payment grant. The user approves it in the wallet, and you continue the grant with the `interact_ref`.
  5. Create the outgoing payment.
- **References:** [openpayments.dev/es](https://openpayments.dev/es) and the [open-payments-node](https://github.com/interledger/open-payments-node) repo. For end-to-end examples, see [Interledger Boutique](https://boutique.interledger-test.dev/) and [Interledger Pay](https://interledgerpay.com/).

- **Get one payment working end to end first.** The organizers say this too, and it's the core of both the "Open Payments usage" criterion and the required demo.

# Cuota Viva: Sales-Based Microloans for Tiendas de Barrio

Hackathon MVP guide (working name). RePPIT at 60%: Research, Propose, Plan.

**One-liner:** 10% of every digital sale repays the loan the moment it lands, with a daily cap the tendero approves once in their own wallet.

---

## 1. The Hook (Research)

**What it solves.** A tendero's income arrives in small, uneven amounts across Nequi, Daviplata, bank transfers, and cash, so a fixed monthly cuota is a bet they often lose. Banks turn them down for lack of credit history, which leaves the gota a gota: lenders reported at 20% to 40% per month who collect in person. The lender's problem is the same thing seen from the other side. It can't see or collect revenue that's spread across wallets, so it turns the store down or prices in the expected default.

**Why Open Payments / ILP.**

- **One integration, many wallets.** Every wallet provider that implements Open Payments exposes the same wallet address, quote, and outgoing payment resources. The lender integrates once, not once per wallet.
- **Consent with a hard ceiling.** The tendero approves one interactive grant: "this lender may debit up to COP 20,000 per day." The merchant's wallet enforces that limit, so the lender's code can't take more. This is the trust story for the judges.
- **Micropayments are normal.** A COP 800 deduction doesn't pay for itself on card rails. On ILP it's an ordinary payment.
- **Every repayment is a receipt.** Each repayment has an outgoing payment ID, and the lender's incoming payment keeps a running `receivedAmount`. Together they form an audit trail that lives on the rails, not only in our database.

**Pitch caveat:** this assumes the store's wallet providers support Open Payments. In the demo, the merchant and the lender use Interledger test-network wallets, and the sales channels are labels on simulated events.

---

## 2. Solution and Demo Story (Propose)

### The mechanism

One rule, applied to every sale:

```
deduction = min( 10% of sale + carried amount,  remaining balance,  today's cap left )
```

- **Under COP 1,000:** carry it to the next sale instead of sending it. Carrying only batches small payments. It doesn't create debt, because the balance is the only debt.
- **COP 1,000 or more:** get a quote, then pay from the merchant's wallet to the lender's incoming payment for this loan, using the standing grant.
- **No sales, no payment.** Nothing runs on a schedule, so there's no payment to miss and nothing to overdraw.
- **At COP 0:** the engine stops and cancels the grant, so the lender loses debit access automatically.

Demo parameters: loan COP 200,000 (~USD 50), rate 10%, daily cap COP 20,000, minimum payment COP 1,000. The demo shows principal only, with no interest accruing (see the usury answer in section 4).

### The 3-minute demo

Framing for the judges: **the sale is simulated, but the repayment is a real Open Payments payment on the test network.**

| Time | On screen | Balance (COP) | Say |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Doña Rosa's dashboard: loan 200,000, 10%, cap 20,000/day | 200,000 | "Her gota a gota charged 20% a month. This loan moves with her sales." |
| 0:25 | The consent screen she approved in her wallet, with the daily limit | 200,000 | "She signed once. Her wallet enforces the cap, not us." |
| 0:50 | Sale 1: Nequi, 45,000. Deducts 4,500, and the payment ID appears | 195,500 | "Ten percent, paid the second the sale lands." |
| 1:15 | Sale 2: Daviplata, 8,000. The 800 is carried | 195,500 | "Too small to send. We carry it: no fee, no crash." |
| 1:35 | Sale 3: transfer, 120,000. Deducts 12,000 plus the 800 carried | 182,700 | "Three channels, one loan." |
| 1:55 | Replay Sale 3's webhook. Shows "duplicate, 0 charged" | 182,700 | "Networks retry. We never charge twice." |
| 2:15 | Sale 4: Nequi, 60,000. Only 2,700 left under today's cap | 180,000 | "Cap reached. She keeps everything else she sells today." |
| 2:35 | Click "Next day": zero sales, 0 due, loan still current. Switch to the lender's wallet: it received 20,000, which matches the ledger | 180,000 | "Bad day, no penalty. And the lender's wallet matches our ledger to the peso." |

Record a backup video of the full run in case the test network is slow on stage.

---

## 3. Lean Architecture and Data (Plan)

```
 Simulator buttons                 ┌─────────────────────────┐
 (Nequi / Daviplata / Transfer) ─▶ │ 1. Sales Ingestor       │  POST /api/sales/webhook
                                   │    idempotent insert    │
                                   └────────────┬────────────┘
                                                ▼
                                   ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                   │ 2. Quota & Ledger       │  10% rule, caps, balance
                                   │    one queue/merchant   │
                                   └────────────┬────────────┘
                                                ▼
                                   ┌─────────────────────────┐  quote + outgoing payment
                                   │ 3. OP Dispatcher        │ ───────────▶ Merchant wallet ──ILP──▶ Lender wallet
                                   └────────────┬────────────┘              (consented grant)        (incoming payment per loan)
                                                ▼
                         Dashboard (live updates) ◀── GET /api/merchants/:id/loan-status
```

| Component | Job | Rule that matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Sales Webhook Ingestor | Accepts sale events, stores each one once, queues it | Idempotent on `(merchant_id, source_event_id)` |
| 2. Quota & Dynamic Ledger Engine | Applies the rule, writes the repayment, updates the balance in one transaction | One queue per merchant, so two sales can't race on the balance |
| 3. Open Payments / ILP Dispatcher | Creates a quote and an outgoing payment from the merchant's wallet to the lender's incoming payment | Never retries a repayment that is already `completed` |

**Stack:** Node, Express, better-sqlite3, `@interledger/open-payments`, and one HTML dashboard updated with server-sent events. Runs on localhost for the demo.

### Schema (3 tables)

The MVP allows one active loan per merchant, so the loan fields sit on the merchant row. Amounts are integers in the wallet's minor units.

```sql
CREATE TABLE merchants (
  id                  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name                TEXT NOT NULL,
  wallet_address      TEXT NOT NULL,              -- merchant's Open Payments wallet address URL
  grant_token         TEXT,                       -- outgoing-payment token from the consented grant
  grant_manage_url    TEXT,                       -- token rotation, and grant cancel on payoff
  lender_incoming_url TEXT,                       -- lender's incoming payment for this loan
  asset_code          TEXT NOT NULL,
  asset_scale         INTEGER NOT NULL,
  principal_minor     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  balance_minor       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  pending_minor       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- carried sub-threshold amount
  rate_bps            INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1000,
  daily_cap_minor     INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sales_events (
  id              INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  merchant_id     TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES merchants(id),
  source_event_id TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- sender's event ID, the idempotency key
  channel         TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- nequi | daviplata | transfer
  amount_minor    INTEGER NOT NULL,
  occurred_at     TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (merchant_id, source_event_id)
);

CREATE TABLE repayments (
  id                  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  merchant_id         TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES merchants(id),
  sales_event_id      INTEGER NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES sales_events(id), -- at most one per sale
  debit_minor         INTEGER NOT NULL,           -- taken from the merchant
  received_minor      INTEGER,                    -- landed at the lender, reduces the balance
  quote_id            TEXT,
  outgoing_payment_id TEXT,
  status              TEXT NOT NULL,              -- pending | completed | failed
  created_at          TEXT NOT NULL
);
```

"Collected today" is the sum of today's `pending` and `completed` repayments, where "today" means a day in Bogotá time.

### API contracts

`POST /api/sales/webhook` (example values: COP at assetScale 2)

```json
// request
{ "merchant_id": "rosa-01", "source_event_id": "nequi-7f3a", "channel": "nequi",
  "amount_minor": 4500000, "occurred_at": "2026-11-02T14:05:00-05:00" }

// 202 new sale
{ "status": "accepted", "sale_id": 41, "deduction_minor": 450000, "repayment_status": "pending" }

// 200 replayed sale
{ "status": "duplicate", "sale_id": 41, "deduction_minor": 0 }
```

`GET /api/merchants/:id/loan-status` (state at the end of the demo)

```json
{ "merchant_id": "rosa-01", "principal_minor": 20000000, "balance_minor": 18000000,
  "repaid_pct": 10.0, "pending_minor": 0,
  "today": { "sales_minor": 23300000, "collected_minor": 2000000, "cap_left_minor": 0 },
  "on_rails_received_minor": 2000000,
  "recent": [{ "sale_id": 44, "channel": "nequi", "debit_minor": 270000,
               "status": "completed", "outgoing_payment_id": "https://..." }] }
```

`on_rails_received_minor` is read live from the `receivedAmount` on the lender's incoming payment. Showing it next to the ledger balance is the "ledger matches the rails" moment.

### Dispatcher call sequence

```js
import { createAuthenticatedClient } from '@interledger/open-payments';

const client = await createAuthenticatedClient({
  walletAddressUrl: LENDER_WALLET, keyId: KEY_ID, privateKey: PRIVATE_KEY_PATH,
});

// Once, at loan origination: the tendero consents in their wallet (interactive grant).
const merchant = await client.walletAddress.get({ url: MERCHANT_WALLET });
const pending = await client.grant.request({ url: merchant.authServer }, {
  access_token: { access: [{
    type: 'outgoing-payment', actions: ['create', 'read'], identifier: merchant.id,
    limits: {
      debitAmount: { value: String(DAILY_CAP_MINOR), assetCode: merchant.assetCode, assetScale: merchant.assetScale },
      interval: 'R/2026-11-02T05:00:00Z/P1D', // resets at midnight Bogotá
    },
  }] },
  interact: { start: ['redirect'], finish: { method: 'redirect', uri: CALLBACK_URL, nonce: NONCE } },
});
// Send the tendero to pending.interact.redirect. On callback with interact_ref:
const grant = await client.grant.continue(
  { url: pending.continue.uri, accessToken: pending.continue.access_token.value }, { interact_ref });
// Store grant.access_token.value and grant.access_token.manage on the merchant row.

// Per repayment: quote from the merchant's wallet, then pay with the stored grant.
const quote = await client.quote.create({ url: merchant.resourceServer, accessToken: QUOTE_TOKEN }, {
  walletAddress: merchant.id, receiver: LENDER_INCOMING_URL, method: 'ilp',
  debitAmount: { value: String(deduction), assetCode: merchant.assetCode, assetScale: merchant.assetScale },
});
const payment = await client.outgoingPayment.create({ url: merchant.resourceServer, accessToken: GRANT_TOKEN }, {
  walletAddress: merchant.id, quoteId: quote.id, metadata: { saleId },
});
// Credit the ledger with quote.receiveAmount, not the debit amount.
```

`QUOTE_TOKEN` comes from a non-interactive `quote` grant on the merchant's auth server. `LENDER_INCOMING_URL` is created once per loan on the lender's resource server, with `incomingAmount` set to the payoff amount. It completes when the loan is paid off, so it doubles as the payoff receipt on the rails.

### Build order

1. **Spike first:** make one outgoing payment between two test wallets through the SDK. Everything else is ordinary web code. This is the part that can sink the project.
2. Interactive grant with the daily limit, the callback handler, and token storage.
3. Ingestor and engine, including the two edge cases below.
4. Dashboard with live updates and simulator buttons (Sale, Replay, Next day).
5. Backup video.

**Demo-day gotchas:** access tokens expire, so rotate them through the manage URL before going on stage. Set `expiresAt` on the lender's incoming payment to the loan's maximum term. Pre-fund the merchant's test wallet, because a simulated sale doesn't put test money into it.

---

## 4. Edge Cases: Build vs. Backlog (Plan)

### Build 1: zero-sales days and tiny sales

Nothing runs unless a sale comes in, so a zero-sales day can't trigger a payment. Zero, negative, or junk amounts deduct nothing. Small amounts carry forward, and no deduction can exceed the balance or the cap. A final payment below the minimum still goes through. If a payment fails, for example because the wallet lacks funds, it's marked `failed` and the balance stays untouched.

```js
function computeDeduction(saleAmount, loan, collectedToday) {
  if (!(saleAmount > 0) || loan.balance <= 0) return 0;                       // zero/junk sale or paid off
  const raw = Math.floor(saleAmount * loan.rateBps / 10_000) + loan.pending;
  const due = Math.min(raw, loan.balance, loan.dailyCap - collectedToday);    // never above balance or cap
  if (due < MIN_PAYMENT && due < loan.balance) { loan.pending = Math.max(due, 0); return 0; } // carry it
  loan.pending = 0; return due;
}
```

### Build 2: duplicate webhooks

```js
const row = db.prepare(`INSERT INTO sales_events (merchant_id, source_event_id, channel, amount_minor, occurred_at)
  VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT (merchant_id, source_event_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING id`)
  .get(merchantId, sourceEventId, channel, amountMinor, occurredAt);
if (!row) return res.status(200).json({ status: 'duplicate', deduction_minor: 0 }); // replay: ack, never re-charge
enqueueDeduction(merchantId, row.id); // second guard: repayments.sales_event_id is UNIQUE
```

### Backlog: judge Q&A (explain, don't code)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How do you stop fake or circular sales? | Fake sales don't help on repayment: they only make the merchant pay off faster at the same rate. The real risk is in underwriting, so in production we size credit lines only from sales the merchant's wallet actually received over several weeks, raise lines only after on-time cycles, and flag bursts of sales and same-day round trips. |
| How do you stay under the tasa de usura? | The Superintendencia Financiera certifies a usury cap for each credit type, set at 1.5 times the interés bancario corriente, and charging above it is a crime. A flat fee breaks the cap when a merchant repays fast, because the effective annual rate shoots up, so we charge daily interest on the outstanding balance at a rate below the current cap, which stays compliant however fast they repay. |
| What about returns and chargebacks? | The payer pushes Open Payments transfers and they're final, so these rails have no card-style chargeback, and a refund is a new payment from the merchant to the customer. The engine records the refund as a negative sale and subtracts the 10% taken on that sale from the next deductions, so the merchant never repays on revenue they gave back. |
| Most tienda sales are cash. Doesn't that break it? | Deductions apply only to digital sales, which keeps the merchant in control of what they commit. It also builds in an incentive: more digital sales mean a verified sales history, and that history unlocks a bigger line next time. |
| What if a wallet provider doesn't support Open Payments? | We can't collect from that wallet yet, but the loan still works through the wallets that do support it. A provider can add support with Rafiki, the Interledger Foundation's open-source implementation. |

---

## 5. Impact and Value Creation

**Market.** Fenalco estimates about 450,000 tiendas de barrio, and some estimates run near 500,000 because many stores aren't formally registered. They handle about 48% of mass-consumption sales, and 90% or more of households buy from them. Check the primary Fenalco source before putting these on a slide.

| Who | Today | With Cuota Viva | Metric to show |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tendero | Gota a gota at 20% to 40% a month, which compounds to about 792% to 5,569% a year. Fixed payments, collected in person | Rate at or below the SFC cap. Payments move with sales, and a zero-sales day means a zero payment. No collector at the door | Effective annual rate vs. the current cap. Share of sales deducted (target 10%) |
| Lender | Can't see revenue split across wallets. Collects by hand and prices in the expected default | Collects automatically, at the moment the cash exists. Slowing sales give early warning before a default | Collection rate (repaid ÷ due), cost per collection, days to payoff |
| Credit system | The tendero has no credit file | Every repayment has an Open Payments receipt. After a few cycles the merchant has a verifiable history that can support a bigger line or formal credit | Repayment cycles with complete receipts on the rails |

Annual figures are compounded from the monthly rates: 1.20¹² − 1 ≈ 792% and 1.40¹² − 1 ≈ 5,569%. Put the SFC's current certified usury rate next to them on the slide.

**Closing line:** "The gota a gota collects at the door every day. Cuota Viva collects only when she sells, and never more than she agreed to."

---

**Sources**

- [Fenalco store count and household share (Portafolio)](https://www.portafolio.co/negocios/comercio/dia-del-tendero-el-90-de-los-hogares-compra-en-tiendas-de-barrio-que-esperan-el-fin-de-los-impuestos-saludables-501371)

content.text:
I've read the Cuota Viva plan and haven't changed anything in the repo. The idea fits the judging criteria well: inclusion, impact, and a payment flow that's built on Open Payments rather than added at the end. The flow (lender client → interactive outgoing-payment grant on the merchant's auth server → quote grant → incoming payment per loan) is the standard third-party Open Payments pattern, so the design holds up. Here's what I'd check before writing code, most important first:

### Problems that could break the demo
1. **The grant interval starts in the future.** The interval in the code is `R/2026-11-02T05:00:00Z/P1D` and the example dates are November, but the hackathon is Oct 16–17. If the wallet treats the grant as not yet active, every payment will be rejected. Start the interval at a recent past Bogotá midnight, for example `R/2026-10-16T05:00:00Z/P1D`.
2. **COP may not be supported on the test wallet.** Check this in the spike. If COP isn't offered, or the two wallets use different currencies, quotes will include FX and fees. Then `receiveAmount` won't equal `debitAmount`, and the "matches to the peso" numbers in the table won't come out exact. The safest setup is both wallets in the same currency, with COP shown only as a display label if needed.
3. **"Next day" is simulated but the wallet's cap is not.** The wallet resets the daily limit in real time, not when you click the button. Your script survives this because the next day has zero sales. But if anyone makes a sale after "Next day", the wallet will reject it because the cap is already used up. Either keep the script exactly as written, or have "Next day" request a fresh grant.
4. **Creating an outgoing payment doesn't mean it's completed.** The create call returns before the money moves. The dispatcher has to poll `outgoingPayment.get` until it sees the final state (`failed` or the full `sentAmount`) before setting status to `completed`. Credit the ledger from what actually landed, not from `quote.receiveAmount`. Without polling, the payment ID will show on screen before the payment has finished.
5. **Access tokens expire quickly on the test network.** The plan already mentions rotation. I'd build `token.rotate` into the dispatcher so it retries once on a 401, rather than doing it by hand before going on stage.

### Smaller logic points
- **In `computeDeduction`:** once the cap is reached, `pending` is reset to 0, so the carried amount disappears. Also, if a payment fails, the amount that was already carried is lost. That matches "she keeps everything else", but decide whether it's intentional.
- **The 3-minute demo** has to fit inside the 5-minute slot for pitch and demo together, so the pitch only gets about 2 minutes.
- **The doc itself:** if this design doc was written with AI help, mention it in `AI_USAGE.md`.

### Build order
I agree with putting the spike first. The first task I'd suggest is a standalone script that makes one payment between two test wallets: get the quote grant, create the incoming payment, get the interactive grant with the limits and interval, then create the outgoing payment. That one script also answers points 1, 2 and 4. For it, each of you needs two test wallet accounts (a merchant and a lender), plus a key ID and private key for the lender.

I've added a short summary of the idea to my project memory. Send me the first task when you're ready.

content.text:
You can run `app.py` without installing anything. The Python environment is already set up. You only need a callback URL that points at your own machine, and access to a sender wallet. I haven't modified any tracked file. The one leftover is described under "Something I changed" at the end.

### What's in `dev-simon`
The branch is at the same commit as `main`. It's a **Python FastAPI** app built on the Interledger Python SDK (`open-payments-sdk`, installed from GitHub), not the Node stack in the design doc.

| Endpoint | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /keys/generate` | Creates an Ed25519 key pair for a wallet, saves it in `src/keys_store.json`, and returns `public_key_b64` for you to paste into the Test Wallet |
| `POST /payments/initiate` | Does the full setup: incoming-payment grant → incoming payment on the receiver → quote grant → quote → interactive outgoing-payment grant. It returns the `redirect_url` where the payer approves |
| `GET /callback/{order_id}` | Where the wallet sends the browser after approval. It continues the grant and creates the outgoing payment |

### What's already installed (all checked)
- `.venv` exists with Python 3.13 and every dependency, including the SDK. Imports work.
- `uv sync --locked --dry-run` reports "Would make no changes", so the lockfile matches.
- The SDK methods the code calls exist in the installed SDK version, and the app loads with all three routes.
- Not installed: **ngrok** and **ruff**. Ruff only matters for linting; `uvx ruff check .` runs it without installing.

### How to run it
1. **Start the server from inside `src/`.** `keys_store.json` is opened by a relative path, so the `uv run uvicorn app:app --app-dir src` command in `CLAUDE.md`, run from the repo root, won't find it. You'll get "No key registered". (The VS Code launch config already uses `src` as its working directory.)
   ```fish
   cd src
   env CALLBACK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/callback uv run uvicorn app:app --reload
   ```
2. **Use your own callback URL.** `src/.env` currently points `CALLBACK_BASE_URL` at an ngrok tunnel, probably a teammate's. The approval would then redirect to their server, which doesn't have your pending payment in memory, and you'd get a 404. You don't need ngrok, because the redirect happens in your own browser, so `localhost` works. `load_dotenv` doesn't override a variable that's already set, which is why the `env …` prefix above works without editing `.env`.
3. **Choose a sender wallet.** `keys_store.json` already has keys for two wallets, `…/8232da3e` and `…/5d4b8d27`.
   - If you can log into the Test Wallet account that owns one of them, use it as the sender. You have to log in as the sender to approve.
   - To use your own wallet, call `POST /keys/generate` and paste `public_key_b64` into Test Wallet → Developer Keys. **That call writes to `src/keys_store.json`, which is tracked by git, so it changes the repo.** Tell me when you're ready for that.
4. **Make the payment.**
   - Call `POST /payments/initiate` with `{order_id, amount_value, sender_wallet, receiver_wallet}`. `amount_value` is in the receiver's minor units, so `"1000"` means 10.00.
   - Open the `redirect_url` and approve in the sender's wallet.
   - The callback returns the `payment_id`. `/docs` gives you a Swagger UI for the POST calls.

### Problems I noticed, for the team to fix
1. **Private keys are committed.** `src/keys_store.json` holds PEM private keys and has been tracked since commit `27a8325`. The repo has to be public by Saturday at 11:00, which would publish them. They're test wallets only, but it breaks the `CLAUDE.md` rule. Remove the file from git, add it to `.gitignore`, and rotate the keys. Deleting it now won't remove the keys from git history.
2. **The outgoing grant goes to the wrong auth server.** `open_payment.py:126` requests it from the **receiver's** auth server; it should be the sender's. It only works because every test wallet shares one auth server.
3. **The sender is always the key owner.** `client_wallet_address` is used as both the API client and the payer. In Cuota Viva the client is the lender and the payer is the merchant, so this needs refactoring later.
4. **"completed" is reported without checking.** The callback returns `"completed"` without reading the payment's final state.
   - `pending_payments` is held in memory, so it's lost when the server restarts.
   - The `hash` parameter on the callback is never verified.
5. **`requirements.txt` lacks `open-payments-sdk`.** Anyone installing with pip instead of uv won't get the SDK.
6. **The two key wallets weren't checked.** I tried to confirm `8232da3e` and `5d4b8d27` still resolve on the test network, but the permission check blocked the request, so I don't know.

### Something I changed
The import check created `src/__pycache__/` and `src/interfaces/__pycache__/`. They're git-ignored, and running the server creates them anyway. I tried to delete them, but the permission check blocked it. To remove them yourself: `rm -r src/__pycache__ src/interfaces/__pycache__`.

content.text:
## Daily-cap consent in Open Payments: how it works and where it goes

### 1. The mechanism
The hard ceiling is set by the `limits` object on the **outgoing-payment grant**. It isn't a separate feature. The installed Python SDK already models it as `LimitsOutgoing` in `open_payments_sdk/models/auth.py:192`:

```json
"limits": {
  "receiver":    "<lender incoming payment URL for this loan>",
  "debitAmount": { "value": "2000000", "assetCode": "COP", "assetScale": 2 },
  "interval":    "R/2026-10-16T05:00:00Z/P1D"
}
```

| Field | Meaning | For Cuota Viva |
|---|---|---|
| `debitAmount` | The most that can be debited from the merchant per interval, added up across **all** payments under the grant | The daily cap (20,000.00 COP is `"2000000"` at scale 2) |
| `interval` | ISO 8601 repeating interval. When a new period starts, the amount spent resets to 0 | `R/<start>/P1D` means every day, forever. Midnight in Bogotá is `05:00Z` (UTC−5, no daylight saving) |
| `receiver` | Payments under the grant can only go to this incoming payment | The lender's incoming payment for this loan. The grant can't pay anyone else |
| `receiveAmount` | Alternative cap measured on the receiver's side | Don't use it; cap on `debitAmount`, since that's what the tendero sees |

What each combination means:
- **No `interval`:** `debitAmount` is a one-time total for the whole life of the grant.
- **With `interval`:** `debitAmount` applies per day, which is what you want.
- **All three together:** the grant reads as "this platform may pay *only this loan*, *at most 20,000 a day*."

The merchant's wallet (its auth server and resource server) enforces this, not your code. When an outgoing payment would push the day's total over the cap, the resource server rejects it, so your code can't overcharge even if it has a bug. This is the "hard ceiling" in your pitch.

Two caveats on the interval:
- **Start date:** use a start that's already in the past, like today's Bogotá midnight. The design doc's `2026-11-02` is in the future and may make the grant unusable today.
- **Real time:** the wallet resets the cap on the real clock, so the simulated "Next day" button won't reset it.

### 2. The actors (with the "client" approach)
| Role | Who | Needs keys? |
|---|---|---|
| **Client** | The Cuota Viva platform (or the lender), with its own test wallet address and a developer key | **Yes.** Every request is signed with this key |
| **Sender** | The tendero's wallet | **No.** The tendero only logs in to their wallet once to approve |
| **Receiver** | The lender's wallet, which holds one incoming payment per loan | No |

This change also fixes the current code's assumption that client = sender (`client_wallet_address` is used as the payer). From now on, use `client_wallet_address` only in the `"client"` field of grant requests. The payer is the merchant's wallet address, and it goes in `identifier` and `walletAddress`.

### 3. The full flow

**Phase A: Loan origination (once per loan, the only step that needs the tendero)**

```
Platform (client)                Lender wallet AS/RS        Merchant wallet AS/RS          Tendero (browser)
 1. GET merchant wallet address ───────────────────────────────▶ (authServer, resourceServer, assetCode, assetScale)
 2. GET lender wallet address ───▶
 3. POST grant {incoming-payment, create/read}  (non-interactive)
                                ◀── access_token
 4. POST /incoming-payments {incomingAmount = payoff, expiresAt = loan term}
                                ◀── lender_incoming_url
 5. POST grant {outgoing-payment, limits{receiver, debitAmount=cap, interval}, interact{redirect, finish{uri, nonce}}}
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ merchant AS
                                                               ◀── interact.redirect, interact.finish, continue{uri, access_token}
 6. Send the tendero to interact.redirect ─────────────────────────────────────────────▶ logs in, sees the limits, approves
 7. Wallet redirects the browser to finish_uri?interact_ref=…&hash=…  ◀────────────────────
 8. Verify hash  →  POST continue{uri} {interact_ref}  ────────▶ merchant AS
                                                               ◀── access_token{value, manage, expires_in} + continue{uri, access_token}
 9. Persist all of it on the loan/merchant record
```

**Phase B: Each sale (no user interaction, repeated as often as needed)**

```
10. POST grant {quote, create/read} on merchant AS (non-interactive, cheap; request a fresh one each time)
11. POST /quotes on merchant RS {walletAddress: merchant, receiver: lender_incoming_url, method: ilp, debitAmount: deduction}
12. POST /outgoing-payments on merchant RS {walletAddress: merchant, quoteId}  using the STORED outgoing token
      ├─ cap OK    → 201, payment created
      └─ over cap  → rejected (4xx, "insufficient grant"); treat it as "cap reached", not as a crash
13. GET /outgoing-payments/{id} until it finishes: check failed / sentAmount
14. Ledger: subtract the amount that actually arrived (sentAmount, or the lender incoming payment's receivedAmount)
```

**Phase C: Keeping the grant alive, and ending it**

```
15. Token expired (401)   → POST manage URL (rotate) with the current token → new token value + new manage URL. Store both.
16. Loan paid off          → DELETE continue URI with the continue token → grant revoked; the platform can't debit any more
```

### 4. What to store after step 8
The design doc only stores `grant_token` and `grant_manage_url`. Revoking the grant at payoff also needs the **continue** values:

| Field | From | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `access_token.value` | continuation response | Authorization for each outgoing payment |
| `access_token.manage` | continuation response | Rotating the token (step 15) |
| `access_token.expires_in` | continuation response | Rotating before it expires |
| `continue.uri` + `continue.access_token.value` | continuation response | Revoking the grant at payoff (step 16) |
| `lender_incoming_url` | step 4 | `receiver` limit and quote receiver |
| `nonce` + `interact.finish` | steps 5 and 6 (temporary) | Hash check in step 8 |

### 5. How it maps to the SDK
- **Grant request:** use the same `GrantRequest(**{...})` pattern as now (`open_payment.py:127`), and add `"interval"` to `limits`. Request it from the **merchant's** auth server. Today `open_payment.py:126` asks the receiver's auth server, which is a bug; it works only because every test wallet shares one auth server.
- **Hash check:** `open_payments_sdk/gnap_utils/hash.py` has `HashManager().verify_hash(client_nonce, interact_nonce, interact_ref, auth_server_url, received_hash)`. `interact_nonce` is `outgoing_grant.root.interact.finish`. The callback currently ignores `hash`.
- **Continuation:** `client.grants.post_grant_continuation_request(...)` is already in use. Return the **whole** grant, not just `.access_token.value`.
- **Rotation:** `client.access_tokens.post_rotate_access_token(token_id, auth_server_endpoint, access_token)`. The SDK builds the URL as `{auth_server}/token/{token_id}`, so `token_id` is the last path segment of the `manage` URL.
- **Revocation:** `client.grants.delete_grant(...)` sends a DELETE to `{auth_server}/continue/{id}`. Pass the id from `continue.uri` and use the continue token.
- **Remaining cap:** the create-payment response includes `grantSpentDebitAmount`, which is how much of today's cap has been used. The SDK parses the response into `OutgoingPayment`, and the repo's patch sets `extra="ignore"`, so that field is thrown away. If you want to show "cap left" from the wallet itself, read it from the raw JSON. Otherwise compute it from your own ledger.

### 6. Where it goes in the code
- **`interfaces/open_payment.py`** (the Open Payments layer):
  - `request_capped_outgoing_grant(merchant_wallet, lender_incoming_url, cap, asset, interval, finish_uri, nonce)`
  - `continue_grant(...)`, returning the full grant
  - `rotate_token(...)` and `revoke_grant(...)`
  - Change `create_quote` and `create_outgoing_payment` to take the merchant wallet as a parameter instead of using `client_wallet_address`.
  - The quote needs a `debitAmount`, the per-sale deduction. The lender's incoming payment has a fixed payoff amount, so leaving the quote's amount empty would try to pay off the whole loan in one payment.
- **`app.py`:**
  - `POST /loans` runs steps 1–6 and returns the redirect URL.
  - `GET /callback/{loan_id}` runs steps 7–9.
  - The sales engine runs steps 10–14 with the stored token.
- **Persistence:** `pending_payments` is held in memory, which is fine for the short gap between steps 5 and 8. The approved grant has to survive restarts, though, so keep it in SQLite or a JSON file. Keep that file out of git, the same as the keys.

### 7. Check in the first spike
1. Does the test wallet's consent screen show the amount and the interval? This is your demo moment at 0:25.
2. What exact error does a payment over the cap return? Make it fail on purpose with a small cap, such as 5.00, and two payments.
3. What `expires_in` do the test wallet's tokens have? Does rotation still work after a token has expired?
4. Is COP available on the test wallet? If not, use the same currency on both wallets so the demo numbers come out exact.

Tell me when the client refactor is ready and I'll review it against this flow.

content.text:
Both changes improve the idea: sales are now real payments you can see, and each repayment comes out of money that just arrived. There's one ambiguity to settle before you code, and a few consequences to plan for.

## 1. A wallet the platform controls
**What you gain**
- **Real sales instead of simulated ones.** Every customer payment is an incoming payment on that wallet, so the platform can see it. The "the sale is simulated" caveat from the demo disappears.
- **Payments almost never fail.** You deduct right after a sale lands, so the money is already in the wallet. The "insufficient funds" case becomes very rare, and that's worth saying in the pitch.

**Keep the tendero's consent.** If the platform also holds the login to that wallet, the platform approves its own grant. Then "she signed once, her wallet enforces the cap" is no longer true. On the test network, set it up like this:
- The **tendero** has their own Test Wallet account, and the "Cuota Viva wallet" is a wallet address inside that account.
- The **platform** is only the client, with its own key. The tendero still logs in once to approve the interactive grant.
- In your app it can still feel like a wallet built into the product. The point is that the account belongs to the tendero.

**How the platform finds out about a sale.** Rafiki webhooks go only to the wallet operator (the test wallet itself), not to third-party clients like yours. So you have to **poll**, and you have two options:

| | (a) Platform creates each charge | (b) Watch the wallet |
|---|---|---|
| How | The tendero taps "cobrar 4.000". The platform creates an incoming payment on the tendero's wallet and shows a QR code or link, then polls that one payment until `receivedAmount` arrives | Poll `GET /incoming-payments` on the tendero's wallet, which the SDK supports with `get_incoming_payments` |
| Grant | `incoming-payment` with `create` and `read` | You need `list-all` and `read-all`, because without them a client only sees payments it created itself. Payments created from the wallet UI wouldn't show up |
| Pros and cons | Each payment maps exactly to one sale, and you get a "cobro con QR" feature too. The customer has to pay through Open Payments | Any payment counts, but you have to filter out ones that aren't sales |

I recommend **(a)** for the hackathon. It's deterministic, easy to demo, and tells a good story. Whichever you choose, **don't count the loan disbursement as a sale**. It lands in the same wallet, so mark it (in its `metadata` or by remembering its ID) so you don't take 10% of the loan itself.

## 2. Per-sale micropayments
This works. In Open Payments terms, every sale triggers a quote, then an outgoing payment from the tendero's wallet to the lender's incoming payment for this loan, using the stored grant token. ILP already splits payments into packets internally, so you don't build any "streaming" yourself. Each deduction is just a normal outgoing payment.

Some practical points:
- **Each deduction costs about 3 signed requests** (quote grant, quote, outgoing payment) plus polling until it completes. One milk sale of about 4,000 COP gives a 400 COP deduction, which works but makes a lot of calls. Keep the carry-forward minimum from the original design. It's still a good idea, even though it isn't required.
- **Process sales one at a time per tendero.** Two milk sales within a second shouldn't both read the same balance.
- **Show the per-sale receipt in the demo.** Sale → deduction → payment ID appearing live is the strongest moment you'll have.

## 3. "When the cap is reached, terminate the grant": which cap?
The answer changes how you build it.

| If "cap" means… | What to do |
|---|---|
| **The daily cap** | **Don't terminate the grant.** With `interval: R/…/P1D` the wallet already blocks payments past the cap and resets it at midnight. If you revoke the grant, the tendero has to approve again every day, and you lose "she signed once". When the wallet refuses a payment over the cap, stop deducting until the next day |
| **The total debt (payoff)** | **Yes, terminate it.** Set the lender's incoming payment `incomingAmount` = payoff. When it completes, revoke the grant (DELETE the continue URI with the continue token). The lender loses debit access automatically, which matches your closing line |

You can combine them, and I'd recommend it: **a daily cap enforced by the wallet's interval, and the grant revoked at payoff**. If you only want a total cap, leave out `interval` and set `debitAmount` = payoff. The grant then runs out by itself, and you still revoke it to clean up.

## 4. Updated flow
```
Onboarding  tendero's wallet (their account) + platform client key
Disburse    lender → tendero wallet (marked as disbursement, not a sale)
Origination incoming payment on lender wallet (incomingAmount = payoff)
            interactive outgoing grant on tendero AS: limits{receiver, debitAmount=daily cap, interval=P1D}
            tendero approves once → store token, manage URL, continue URI + token
Each sale   platform creates "cobro" incoming payment → customer pays → polling sees it completed
            → deduction = % of sale (carry if tiny, ≤ cap left, ≤ balance)
            → quote grant → quote(debitAmount) → outgoing payment with stored token → poll until completed
Cap hit     wallet refuses → stop until tomorrow (no revoke)
Payoff      lender incoming payment completes → revoke grant → loan closed
```

## 5. Pitch questions to prepare for
- **"Who holds the money in that wallet?"** In production, the wallet has to be held at a licensed account provider running Rafiki, because holding customer funds in Colombia requires a licence (SEDPE or a bank). Puntored is a payments company and sponsors the Inclusion prize, so they're a natural partner to name.
- **"Who's the customer in the demo?"** It's a third test wallet, and that wallet has to approve its own payment. Have it logged in on a phone before you go on stage.

Which cap did you mean, daily or total? Once you tell me, I can outline the grant request body and the polling loop for your Python client.

Here's the change in Open Payments terms. The grant stops being "X per day, forever" and becomes **"up to the total debt, for the length of the credit"**, and you revoke it early if the loan is paid off first.

## 1. The grant
```python
"limits": {
    "receiver":    lender_incoming_url,                     # can only pay this loan
    "debitAmount": {"value": payoff_value,                  # total debt (principal + interest), minor units
                    "assetCode": asset_code, "assetScale": asset_scale},
    "interval":    "R1/2026-10-16T05:00:00Z/P1M",           # optional: the credit term (P7D, P1M…)
}
```
- **`debitAmount` with no repeating interval** is a total for the whole life of the grant. The wallet will never let the platform take more than the debt.
- **`receiver`** keeps the grant from paying anyone except this loan.
- **`interval`** is how you tell the wallet itself about the term. I haven't confirmed how Rafiki treats a payment that falls after a non-repeating interval ends. Whether to write `R1/` or `R0/` is also unclear. **Test this in the spike:** create a grant with `P5M` (5 minutes), wait for it to pass, then try to pay.
- **Your own code must also end it.** Check the term on every sale and revoke the grant when it expires. That way the term is enforced whatever the wallet does, and the demo doesn't depend on the interval behaving as expected.

**Back the cap with the incoming payment.** Create the lender's incoming payment with `incomingAmount` = payoff and `expiresAt` = end of term. Once it fills, it won't accept more money. Its `completed` flag is your payoff signal.

## 2. Ways the loan ends
| Event | How you detect it | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Paid off early | Lender incoming payment `completed == True`, or your balance reaches 0 | Revoke the grant, close the loan |
| Term ends with debt left | `now > term_end`, checked on each sale and on a periodic check | Revoke the grant and mark the loan `overdue`. Collections and renegotiation are pitch Q&A, not code |
| Total cap reached | Same as paid off, since cap = debt | Covered by the first row |

## 3. Token lifetime
The grant lasts a month, but the **access token expires much sooner** (check `expires_in`). Every payment call has to handle a 401 by rotating with `client.access_tokens.post_rotate_access_token(...)` and retrying once. Then save the new value **and the new manage URL**. If you skip this, payments start failing a few minutes in, possibly during the demo.

## 4. Where it goes in the code
Based on the current layout. Adapt the names once the client refactor is in.

### `src/interfaces/open_payment.py`: Open Payments calls only, no business logic
The class's own wallet (`client_wallet_address`) is **only** the client. The tendero's wallet comes in as a parameter.

| Method | Calls | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `get_wallet(url)` | `wallet.get_wallet_address` | Rename `discover_receiver_servers`, since it's used for both sides |
| `create_loan_incoming_payment(lender_wallet, payoff, expires_at)` | incoming grant + `incoming_payments.post_create_payment` | `IncomingPaymentRequest` already has `expiresAt` and `metadata` |
| `request_loan_grant(tendero_wallet, lender_incoming_url, payoff, interval, finish_uri, nonce)` | `grants.post_grant_request` on the **tendero's** auth server | Fixes the current bug where `:126` uses the receiver's auth server |
| `continue_loan_grant(pending_grant, interact_ref)` | `grants.post_grant_continuation_request` | Return the **whole** grant: token value, `manage`, `expires_in`, `continue.uri`, `continue.access_token` |
| `create_charge(tendero_wallet, amount)` | incoming grant + incoming payment on the tendero's wallet | The "cobro" for one sale. Its URL goes in a QR code or link |
| `get_incoming(url, token)` | `incoming_payments.get_incoming_payment` | Takes the **ID** (last path segment), not the full URL. Used to poll charges and the payoff |
| `pay_installment(tendero_wallet, lender_incoming_url, deduction, token)` | quote grant → quote → `outgoing_payments.post_create_payment` → poll `get_outgoing_payment` | Build the quote with `QuoteFixedSent` (has `debitAmount`), not `QuoteRequestBase`. Without an amount it tries to pay the whole remaining debt in one go |
| `rotate_token(manage_url, token)` | `access_tokens.post_rotate_access_token` | `token_id` is the last segment of the `manage` URL |
| `revoke_grant(continue_uri, continue_token)` | `grants.delete_grant` | `req_id` is the last segment of `continue.uri` |

### `src/loan_engine.py` (new): pure logic, no HTTP
- `compute_deduction(sale, loan)`: the percentage, the carry-forward minimum, and `min(…, balance)`. No daily cap any more.
- `is_expired(loan, now)` and `is_paid_off(loan)`.
- Because there's no HTTP here, you can unit-test it in seconds without the test network.

### `src/store.py` (new): persistence
- Use SQLite or a JSON file, and keep it **out of git**, the same as the keys.
- Each loan stores:
  - `loan_id`, `tendero_wallet`, `lender_wallet`, `lender_incoming_url`
  - `payoff`, `balance`, `pending_carry`, `term_start`, `term_end`, `status`
  - `access_token`, `manage_url`, `continue_uri`, `continue_token`
- Each charge or sale stores its `incoming_payment_url`, `amount`, `status`, and its deduction's `outgoing_payment_id`.
- `pending_payments` can stay in memory, but only for the few minutes between the grant request and the callback.

### `src/models.py`
- `CreateLoanRequest`: `loan_id`, `tendero_wallet`, `lender_wallet`, `principal_value`, `term` (`"P7D"`, `"P1M"`)
- `ChargeRequest`: `loan_id`, `amount_value`

### `src/app.py`: thin endpoints that wire it all together
| Endpoint | Does |
|---|---|
| `POST /loans` | Creates the lender incoming payment, then requests the loan grant. Returns `redirect_url` for the tendero to approve |
| `GET /callback/{loan_id}` | **Verify `hash`** with `HashManager().verify_hash(nonce, interact.finish, interact_ref, auth_server_url, hash)`. Then continue the grant, store the tokens and set the loan `active` |
| `POST /loans/{id}/charges` | Creates the charge and returns its URL for the QR code |
| Background poller | Runs as a FastAPI `lifespan` task. Every ~2 s it checks pending charges. When one completes, it runs the engine and then `pay_installment`. After each payment it checks payoff and term and revokes the grant if either is reached |
| `GET /loans/{id}` | Dashboard data: balance, % repaid, recent deductions with payment IDs, and the lender incoming payment's live `receivedAmount` |

Process **one loan at a time** in the poller, for example with a lock per loan. That way two sales can't both read the same balance.

## 5. Build order
1. **Spike:** in `open_payment.py`, get one capped grant approved by the tendero, then use the stored token to make **two** small payments with **no** further approval. This proves the core claim.
2. In the same spike:
   - Make a payment past the cap on purpose and note the error the wallet returns.
   - Make a payment after the short `P5M` term ends and note what happens.
   - Rotate the token.
   - Revoke the grant and confirm the next payment is rejected.
3. Write the store and the engine, with unit tests.
4. Add the charge creation and the poller.
5. Build the dashboard, then record the demo and a backup video.

Let's go through it step by step. You may only need one part of what I wrote before.

## 1. What an endpoint is
Your app is a **server**: a program that runs and waits for requests. An **endpoint** is one "door" into that server, and each door does one specific job. A door is identified by two things:

- **A method:** `GET` usually means "give me information", and `POST` means "do something / create something".
- **A path:** the address, for example `/payments/initiate`.

So `POST /payments/initiate` is one endpoint, and `GET /callback/{order_id}` is another.

A restaurant is a useful comparison:

| Restaurant | Your project |
|---|---|
| The **menu**: the list of things customers can ask for | **Endpoints**, in `app.py` |
| What the customer writes on the order | The **input** (request body), defined in `models.py` |
| The **kitchen**, where the real work happens | `interfaces/open_payment.py` |
| The **supplier** the kitchen buys from | The Test Wallet / Open Payments servers on the internet |

Customers never go into the kitchen. They order from the menu, and the waiter takes the order to the kitchen. Your app works the same way: the outside world only calls endpoints, and the endpoints call functions in `open_payment.py`.

**Your job ("organize the endpoints") is to design the menu.** You don't need to cook, which is why `open_payment.py` was confusing: that's your teammates' kitchen. You only need to know which "dishes" (functions) it offers so each endpoint can ask for the right one.

## 2. The endpoints that exist today, in `src/app.py`
In FastAPI, an endpoint is a normal Python function with a **decorator** above it (the line starting with `@`):

```python
@app.post("/payments/initiate")             # ← the door: method POST, path /payments/initiate
def initiate_payment(req: InitiatePaymentRequest):   # ← what the caller must send (defined in models.py)
    client = make_client(req.sender_wallet)
    redirect_url, ... = client.create_payment_request(...)   # ← the waiter takes the order to the kitchen
    return {"redirect_url": ..., "order_id": ...}            # ← what the caller gets back
```

Your app currently has three:

| Endpoint | Who calls it | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /keys/generate` | You, once | Creates the keys the app uses to sign its requests |
| `POST /payments/initiate` | You, or later the frontend | Prepares a payment and returns a link where the payer approves it |
| `GET /callback/{order_id}` | **The wallet**, by redirecting the browser | After the payer approves, finishes the payment |

## 3. One payment, step by step
This is what happens in the current code:

```
1. You call  POST /payments/initiate  with {order_id, amount, sender, receiver}
       │
       ▼  app.py → initiate_payment()
2. The endpoint calls the kitchen:  open_payment.create_payment_request()
       │   which talks to the Test Wallet 5 times (permission, invoice, permission, price quote, ask for approval)
       ▼
3. The endpoint answers you:  {"redirect_url": "https://wallet.interledger-test.dev/..."}
       │
       ▼
4. You open that link, log in to the payer's wallet and click "Accept"
       │
       ▼
5. The wallet sends your browser to  GET /callback/{order_id}?interact_ref=...
       │
       ▼  app.py → payment_callback()
6. The endpoint calls the kitchen again: continue the permission, then send the money
       │
       ▼
7. It answers: {"status": "completed", "payment_id": ...}
```

The endpoints in `app.py` stay short. They receive the input, call the kitchen, and return the result. All the Open Payments complexity is in `open_payment.py`.

## 4. The menu for Cuota Viva
These are the endpoints the new idea needs. The last column is the kitchen function each one calls, which your teammates build.

| # | Endpoint | Who calls it | Input | Returns | Kitchen function |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `POST /loans` | Frontend, when the bank creates the loan | tendero wallet, lender wallet, amount, term (`"P1M"`) | `loan_id` and a link for the tendero to approve | create the loan's incoming payment, then request the capped grant |
| 2 | `GET /callback/{loan_id}` | **The wallet**, after the tendero approves | `interact_ref` and `hash` (the wallet adds these) | "loan active" | continue the grant, then save the tokens |
| 3 | `POST /loans/{loan_id}/charges` | Frontend, when the tendero sells something (e.g. 1 milk) | amount | A payment link or QR code for the customer | create an incoming payment on the tendero's wallet |
| 4 | `GET /loans/{loan_id}` | Frontend dashboard | nothing | Balance, % paid, list of deductions, status | read from the database, plus the lender's incoming payment |
| 5 | `GET /loans/{loan_id}/charges` | Frontend dashboard | nothing | List of sales and how much was deducted from each | read from the database |

One thing has no endpoint because nobody calls it from outside: the **automatic deduction**. When a customer pays, the server notices by itself, by checking every few seconds, and sends the percentage to the debt. Your teammates handle it, or you do later.

Your task, concretely:
1. **`models.py`:** define the inputs, for example `CreateLoanRequest` with `tendero_wallet`, `lender_wallet`, `amount`, `term`.
2. **`app.py`:** write the five endpoint functions with their decorators.
3. **Agree with your teammates** on the names and inputs of the kitchen functions each endpoint will call.

## 5. Working before the kitchen is ready
You can make each endpoint return **fake data** (a "stub") for now:

```python

def get_loan(loan_id: str):
    return {"loan_id": loan_id, "balance": 180000, "paid_pct": 10.0, "status": "active"}  # fake for now
```

The frontend person can then build the dashboard right away. When the kitchen functions are ready, you replace the fake line with the real call. Your menu and their kitchen move forward at the same time.

## 6. Seeing your endpoints
FastAPI generates a test page automatically:

```fish

uv run uvicorn app:app --reload
```

Then open **http://localhost:8000/docs** in your browser. You'll see every endpoint listed, and you can click **"Try it out"** to call one and see its response. The page updates every time you save `app.py`.

For the time-limited grant, your part is mostly in **two endpoints**: creating the loan (`POST /loans`) and the callback. Your teammates write the actual permission request in the kitchen. Here it is in simple terms.

## The idea in one sentence
When the loan is created, the tendero approves once, in their wallet, a permission that says:

> "Cuota Viva may take money from my wallet, **only to pay this loan**, **up to the total debt**, **until the end of the term**."

That permission is the **grant**. "Temporal" means it has an end date (the term), and it also ends early if the debt is fully paid.

## Its life cycle and where each step happens

```
① Create loan        POST /loans                  ← YOUR endpoint
② Tendero approves   (in the wallet website)      ← nothing to code
③ Save permission    GET /callback/{loan_id}      ← YOUR endpoint
④ Use it, sale by sale  (automatic, background)    ← teammates
⑤ End it             debt paid OR term over       ← a check + one kitchen function
```

### ① `POST /loans`: the caller sends the time limit
The term and the amount are inputs, so they go in your model in `models.py`:

```python
class CreateLoanRequest(BaseModel):
    tendero_wallet: str      # who borrows
    lender_wallet: str       # who lends
    amount: str              # total debt, e.g. "20000000" = 200,000.00 COP
    term: str                # how long: "P7D" = 7 days, "P1M" = 1 month, "PT5M" = 5 minutes (for testing)
```

In the endpoint you then:
1. Calculate `term_start` (now) and `term_end` (now + term), and **save them** with the loan.
2. Call the kitchen function that asks for the permission, passing the amount, the term and the callback address.
3. Return the approval link to the caller.

```python
@app.post("/loans")
def create_loan(req: CreateLoanRequest):
    loan_id = ...                          # create an id
    # kitchen: ask the tendero's wallet for the capped, time-limited permission
    redirect_url, pending_grant = client.request_loan_grant(
        tendero_wallet=req.tendero_wallet, amount=req.amount, term=req.term,
        finish_uri=f"{CALLBACK_BASE_URL}/{loan_id}", ...)
    # save: loan_id, amount, term_start, term_end, status="waiting_approval", pending_grant
    return {"loan_id": loan_id, "approve_url": str(redirect_url)}
```

Use `"PT5M"` (5 minutes) while testing. You don't want to wait a month to check that the permission expires.

### ② The tendero approves
They open `approve_url`, log in to their Test Wallet, read the permission and click Accept. You don't code anything for this step.

### ③ `GET /callback/{loan_id}`: save the permission
The wallet sends the browser back to your callback. The endpoint:
1. Calls the kitchen to "continue" the grant. The result is a **token**, which works like a key for taking the money later.
2. **Saves** everything the grant returns: the token, the `manage` URL (used to renew the token), and the `continue` URL and token (used to cancel the permission later).
3. Changes the loan's status to `"active"`.

Losing any of these makes later steps fail. Without the token you can't collect, and without the `continue` data you can't end the grant.

### ④ Using the permission (not your part)
On each sale, the background process uses the saved token to send the percentage. The tendero doesn't approve anything again, which is the whole point of the grant.

### ⑤ Ending the permission
There are two ways the grant should end:

| Situation | How you know | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Debt paid early** | Balance reaches 0 | Call the kitchen function `revoke_grant(...)` with the saved `continue` data → status `"paid"` |
| **Term over** | Current time > `term_end` | Call `revoke_grant(...)` → status `"expired"` |

**The wallet also enforces the limits by itself.** It won't allow more than the total debt, and if the term is in the permission it stops after that date. Your own check is a safety net, and it also updates the loan's status in your app.

For the demo, add one more endpoint so you can show the end without waiting:

| Endpoint | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /loans/{loan_id}/close` | Revokes the grant now. Useful on stage: "loan paid → access removed" |

And in `GET /loans/{loan_id}`, return `term_start`, `term_end` and `status` so the dashboard can show "valid until …" and whether it's active, paid or expired.

## What to ask your teammates for (kitchen functions)
1. `request_loan_grant(tendero_wallet, amount, term, finish_uri, ...)` returns the approval link and the pending grant.
2. `continue_loan_grant(pending_grant, interact_ref)` returns the token, the manage URL, and the continue URL and token.
3. `revoke_grant(continue_uri, continue_token)` ends the permission.

Point them to the request body from my earlier message: `limits` with `receiver`, `debitAmount` = total debt, and `interval` = the term.

## Your checklist
- [ ] `CreateLoanRequest` in `models.py` with `amount` and `term`
- [ ] `POST /loans`: calculate and save `term_end`, call `request_loan_grant`, return the link
- [ ] `GET /callback/{loan_id}`: call `continue_loan_grant`, save all the tokens, set `active`
- [ ] Expiry check: if `now > term_end` or balance is 0, call `revoke_grant` and update the status
- [ ] `POST /loans/{loan_id}/close` for the demo
- [ ] `GET /loans/{loan_id}` returns `term_end` and `status`

Start with stubs (fake returns) and swap in the real kitchen calls when they're ready.

| | 💸 Lending the money (disbursement) | 🔐 Permission to collect (the loan grant) |
|---|---|---|

| Who approves | The **lender**, in the lender's wallet | The **tendero**, in the tendero's wallet |
| Limits | One fixed amount | Up to the total debt, until the end of the term |
| Can the existing endpoints do it? | ✅ **Yes, already** | ❌ **No, you need new ones** |

## 💸 Lending the money: reuse what's there
`POST /payments/initiate` followed by `GET /callback/{order_id}` already does "send X from wallet A to wallet B with approval". Call it with the lender as sender and the tendero as receiver:

```json
POST /payments/initiate
{ "order_id": "loan-001-disburse", "amount_value": "20000000",
  "sender_wallet": "<LENDER wallet>", "receiver_wallet": "<TENDERO wallet>" }
```

Open the `redirect_url`, log in as the lender, and accept. The money arrives in the tendero's wallet. You don't need new code for this.

## 🔐 The loan grant: why the existing endpoints don't fit
The existing flow differs in three ways:
1. **It pays immediately in the callback.** Your callback should only **save** the permission, because there's nothing to pay yet.
2. **It allows one payment of one amount.** You need many payments up to a total, within a time limit.
3. **It discards what you need later.** `continue_outgoing_payment_grant` keeps only the token. You also need the data to renew and cancel the permission.

So you need **two new endpoints** (a create and a callback) and **two new kitchen functions**. Here's each piece.

### Step 1: `models.py`, the request body for creating a loan
```python
class CreateLoanRequest(BaseModel):
    loan_id: str
    tendero_wallet: str
    lender_wallet: str
    amount_value: str        # total debt in minor units: "20000000" = 200,000.00
    term_minutes: int        # 5 for testing, 10080 = 1 week, 43200 = 30 days
```
The term is in minutes so you can test expiry in 5 minutes instead of waiting a month.

### Step 2: `interfaces/open_payment.py`, two new functions
**a) Ask the tendero's wallet for the limited permission.** This is a copy of `request_outgoing_payment_grant` with the limits changed:

```python
def request_loan_grant(self, tendero_wallet, lender_incoming_url, debt_value,
                       asset_code, asset_scale, interval, finish_uri, nonce):
    auth_server = self.discover_receiver_servers(tendero_wallet)["auth_server"]  # TENDERO's server
    grant_req = GrantRequest(**{
        "access_token": {"access": [{
            "type": "outgoing-payment",
            "actions": ["create", "read"],
            "identifier": tendero_wallet,                 # money leaves the TENDERO's wallet
            "limits": {
                "receiver": lender_incoming_url,           # only to this loan
                "debitAmount": {"value": debt_value,       # never more than the debt in total
                                "assetCode": asset_code, "assetScale": asset_scale},
                "interval": interval,                      # only during the term
            },
        }]},
        "client": self.client.client_wallet_address,       # our app (the lender's key, for now)
        "interact": {"start": ["redirect"],
                     "finish": {"method": "redirect", "uri": finish_uri, "nonce": nonce}},
    })
    pending = self.client.grants.post_grant_request(grant_req, auth_server)
    return pending.root.interact.redirect, pending
```

**b) After approval, get the token and keep everything.**
```python
def continue_loan_grant(self, pending_grant, interact_ref):
    cont = pending_grant.root.cont
    final = self.client.grants.post_grant_continuation_request(
        interact_ref=InteractRef(interact_ref=interact_ref),
        continue_uri=str(cont.uri),
        access_token=cont.access_token.value,
    )
    return {
        "access_token": final.access_token.value,          # the "key" to collect each payment
        "manage_url": str(final.access_token.manage),      # to renew the key when it expires
        "expires_in": final.access_token.expires_in,
        "continue_uri": str(cont.uri),                     # to CANCEL the permission later
        "continue_token": cont.access_token.value,
    }
```
The SDK's continue response loses the `continue` field: its model names it `cont`, but the JSON key is `continue`. That's why I take `continue_uri` and `continue_token` from the pending grant instead. Confirm in testing that cancelling works with those values.

### Step 3: `app.py`, the two endpoints
New imports at the top: `import secrets`, `from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone`, `from open_payments_sdk.gnap_utils.hash import HashManager`, and `CreateLoanRequest` from `models`.

```python
loans: dict[str, dict] = {}          # in memory for now; later a database


@app.post("/loans")
def create_loan(req: CreateLoanRequest):
    client = make_client(req.lender_wallet)          # the lender's key signs the requests
    tendero = client.discover_receiver_servers(req.tendero_wallet)
    lender = client.discover_receiver_servers(req.lender_wallet)

    # 1. The loan's "piggy bank" on the lender side. It REUSES existing kitchen functions
    token = client.request_incoming_payment_grant(req.lender_wallet)
    lender_incoming_url, _ = client.create_incoming_payment(
        receiver_wallet=req.lender_wallet, resource_server=lender["resource_server"],
        access_token=token, amount_value=req.amount_value,
        asset_code=lender["asset_code"], asset_scale=lender["asset_scale"],
    )

    # 2. The limited permission on the tendero's wallet
    start = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    nonce = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
    redirect_url, pending = client.request_loan_grant(
        tendero_wallet=req.tendero_wallet,
        lender_incoming_url=lender_incoming_url,
        debt_value=req.amount_value,
        asset_code=tendero["asset_code"], asset_scale=tendero["asset_scale"],
        interval=f"R1/{start:%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ}/PT{req.term_minutes}M",
        finish_uri=f"{CALLBACK_BASE_URL}/loan/{req.loan_id}",
        nonce=nonce,
    )

    loans[req.loan_id] = {
        "tendero_wallet": req.tendero_wallet, "lender_wallet": req.lender_wallet,
        "tendero_auth_server": tendero["auth_server"],
        "lender_incoming_url": lender_incoming_url,
        "debt": req.amount_value, "balance": req.amount_value,
        "term_start": start.isoformat(),
        "term_end": (start + timedelta(minutes=req.term_minutes)).isoformat(),
        "nonce": nonce, "pending_grant": pending,
        "status": "waiting_approval",
    }
    return {"loan_id": req.loan_id, "approve_url": str(redirect_url)}


@app.get("/callback/loan/{loan_id}")
def loan_callback(loan_id: str, interact_ref: str = Query(...), hash: str = Query(...)):
    loan = loans.get(loan_id)
    if loan is None or loan["status"] != "waiting_approval":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=f"No loan waiting approval: '{loan_id}'")

    # Check the redirect really comes from the tendero's wallet
    ok = HashManager().verify_hash(loan["nonce"], loan["pending_grant"].root.interact.finish,
                                   interact_ref, loan["tendero_auth_server"], hash)
    if not ok:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid hash")

    client = make_client(loan["lender_wallet"])
    loan.update(client.continue_loan_grant(loan.pop("pending_grant"), interact_ref))
    loan["status"] = "active"
    return {"loan_id": loan_id, "status": "active", "term_end": loan["term_end"]}
```

The path `/callback/loan/{loan_id}` has two segments after `/callback`, so it doesn't clash with the existing `/callback/{order_id}`. Your `.env` stays as it is.

1. Make sure the **lender** wallet has a key in `keys_store.json`. It's the one signing requests (`make_client(req.lender_wallet)`).
2. Run the server, open `http://localhost:8000/docs`, and call `POST /loans` with `term_minutes: 5`.
3. Open `approve_url`, log in as the **tendero**, and check that the screen shows the limits. Then accept.
4. You should get back `"status": "active"`.

| Symptom | Probable cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Grant request rejected (400) | The wallet doesn't like the `R1/...` interval | Try `R0/...`, or remove `"interval"` for now and enforce the term with `term_end` in your own code |
| "Invalid hash" | The URL format used for the hash check | Print the inputs and compare; temporarily log instead of rejecting so you're not blocked |
| `expires_in` is short (minutes) | Normal | Later, renew the token with `manage_url` before each collection |

### What's still missing (next tasks)
- Using the saved `access_token` to collect a percentage on each sale.
- Cancelling at payoff or at `term_end` with `continue_uri` and `continue_token`.
- Saving `loans` to a file or database. If the server restarts now, active loans are lost.
